observations:
Torah #24 yields 11 bechina edges across 17 nodes in 6 raw connected components, reduced to 3 packages. A thorough scan of the source text for bechina language reveals no cluster of 3 or more concepts that (a) are bechina-linked to each other and (b) fail to fit into one of the existing three packages.

All candidate concepts fall naturally into the existing package structure:

(1) The sfirot-structural vocabulary (נצח הוד יסוד, חסד גבורה תפארת, חכמה בינה דעת, מלכות) — these appear throughout the Torah as the structural anatomy of the divine worlds. In Torah #24, they function as path-markers in the eitza chain (section ג-ד: legs clothe arms, arms clothe CHaBaD) rather than as bechina-equated concepts to each other. None form an independent bechina cluster among themselves in this Torah. The one case where explicit bechina language is used ('שֶׁהֵם הַיָּדַיִם') simply adds ChGT to the ידים-node already in Package 1.

(2) The 'worlds' vocabulary (עשיה, יצירה, בריאה, אצילות) — these appear as waypoints in the ascending/descending chain (section ו-ז: 'מלכות דיצירה נעשה ממנה חכמה בינה דעת דעשיה'; 'מפנימיות מלכות דיצירה, נעשה כתר דעשיה') but are eitza relationships (one world producing the next), not bechina equivalences. They do not form a bechina cluster.

(3) The 'תמורה / היכלי התמורות' concept — while this is bechina-linked to the klipot domain (Package 3), it is a single concept that adds to an existing package rather than seeding an independent new one.

(4) The 'nine heikhalot' (תשעה היכלין) — this is a structural outcome produced by the mochin striking the keter (eitza relationship). The text is clear that the heikhalot are created ('נעשין') by the collision, making this an eitza result, not a bechina identity.

(5) Joy/simcha (שמחה) — while the text has strong bechina language connecting שמחה to לב (Package 2), this adds to an existing package rather than creating a new domain.

The Torah's structure is clearly tripartite in its bechina topology: (1) an upper-intellect domain (Package 1: כתר/מחין/ידים/אמונה), (2) an immanent-presence domain (Package 2: שכינה/לב/שמחת ישראל), and (3) an evil-opposite domain (Package 3: קלipot/excess/sadness/harsh-judgment). This matches the Torah's argument: the mochin and Keter (Pkg 1) are the path toward Ein Sof; the Shekhinah-in-the-heart (Pkg 2) is what is liberated or exiled; and the klipot-as-sadness (Pkg 3) is the exile-force that opposes this liberation. No additional independent conceptual domain emerges from the bechina graph of this Torah.
